title: Seeun Park
text:
Pronounced: “SEH‑n” (“n” as in the end of risen)



I am an applied microeconomist with a PhD in Economics from the University of California, Riverside. My research explores the intersection of health, labor, and public economics, focusing on how policies and regulations shape economic and health outcomes.
I am currently a Visiting Assistant Professor of Economics at Bowdoin College.
Explore this site to learn more about my CV, research, and teaching.

title: Seeun Park
text:
Job Market Paper
When the Youngest Child Ages Out: Caretaker Eligibility and Parental Medicaid Loss
Abstract: Using American Community Survey data from 2014 to 2019, I show that parents in non-expansion states lose Medicaid when their youngest child ages out of dependent-child status, even though their own income and circumstances are unchanged. Event-study and difference-in-differences estimates indicate that parental Medicaid falls by about 11 percentage points after the youngest child ages out. The coverage loss translates into uninsurance and is concentrated among the lowest-income families most exposed to the caretaker eligibility rule.



Working Papers
Coverage Continuity Under the ACA Dependent Coverage Provision | Working paper
Abstract: Using monthly insurance coverage data from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey, I find that the ACA’s dependent-coverage provision improved coverage continuity for young adults entirely through parental employer-sponsored insurance by filling gaps in other coverage. When dependent-only months are excluded, the effect on full-year coverage essentially disappears. I am extending the analysis to the Survey of Income and Program Participation to study how the provision interacted with subsequent ACA coverage policies around the age-26 transition.
Coverage Expansion and Behavioral Health Treatment Supply: Evidence from the Affordable Care Act | Under review
Abstract: Using county-level data from 2004 to 2016, I examine how the ACA affected the supply of behavioral health treatment facilities. Difference-in-differences and event-study estimates show that facility supply increased more in counties with lower pre-ACA saturation, but primarily through growth in markets that already had providers rather than entry into previously unserved areas. The results show that coverage expansion can reshape the supply side while leaving geographic gaps in access intact.
The Effect of Building Affordable Housing on Student Mobility | Working paper
Abstract: Using administrative student address records from North Carolina, I examine whether moving into a Low-Income Housing Tax Credit neighborhood improves residential stability for families with school-age children. Difference-in-differences and event-study estimates compare residential mobility among economically disadvantaged students who move into LIHTC neighborhoods to peers from the same origin block group.



Publications
Park, S., & Go, S. (2018). Children’s Age and the Labor Supply of Married Women in Korea. Journal of Korean Economic Development, 24(4), 23-39.
Park, S., & Go, S. (2018). The Effect of Children’s Age on Married Women’s Career Reinterruption. The Journal of Industrial Distribution & Business, 9(7), 43-52.

title: ECON 101: Statistics for Economics
text:
NoteCourse Overview



This course is the first upper‑division requirement for Economics majors and a prerequisite for Econometrics (Econ 107). Many students find it challenging as the quarter progresses. My goal was to make the material approachable by clarifying key concepts and linking them to broader economic intuition. Through weekly reviews, problem‑set discussions, and concise summary notes, I helped students consolidate core ideas and build confidence with the material.
The handwritten notes below come from discussion sections reviewing key concepts.
